source_meaning: A sailor cries that seeing nothing but sea for so long is driving him mad. He wants to get back on land soon.
independent_English: Aaagh! I'm going out of my mind staring at the sea day after day! I want to get back on land!

source_meaning: A formal report that discontent among the sailors is building, with a suggestion to put into port soon.
independent_English: Admiral, the crew's growing restless. It might be wise to put into port soon.

source_meaning: A measured warning that the crew is becoming more disgruntled, followed by a hesitant suggestion to make a port call.
independent_English: Admiral, the crew's getting more and more upset. Perhaps we should put into port for a while...

source_meaning: The speaker has heard the crew is worn out and tentatively suggests putting into port soon.
independent_English: Admiral, it sounds like the crew's worn out. Don't you think it's about time we put into port?

source_meaning: The speaker notices the sailors all seem tired and asks whether they could put into port soon.
independent_English: Admiral, the whole crew looks worn out. Could we put into port soon?

source_meaning: A blunt warning that the crew will go out of their minds if this continues, then advice to make a port call.
independent_English: Admiral, the crew'll go stir-crazy if we keep this up. I think we ought to put into port for a while.

source_meaning: The older voice observes mounting discontent and advises a stop in port.
independent_English: Admiral, the crew's growing restless. We'd best make a stop in port.

source_meaning: A younger voice is scared by the sailors' bad mood and wants to go to port now.
independent_English: Admiral, everybody's in a bad mood! Can we go into port now? I'm scared!

source_meaning: A sailor has reached his limit and threatens to force the fleet to head to port.
independent_English: I've had enough! I'll make them head for port if I have to!

source_meaning: The crew is on the verge of an angry outburst. The speaker asks the admiral to decide what to do.
independent_English: The crew's about to boil over, Admiral. What should we do?

source_meaning: The speaker warns that the angry sailors look ready to use force and asks what the admiral wants to do.
independent_English: It looks like the crew's ready to use force... What should we do, Admiral?

source_meaning: The speaker realizes the crew is about to erupt and asks the admiral for direction.
independent_English: This is bad... The crew's about to lose it. What do we do, Admiral?

source_meaning: The speaker urgently tells the admiral that the angry crew is about to use force and asks what to do.
independent_English: Admiral, we've got trouble! The crew's furious and ready to use force! What should we do?

source_meaning: A rough voice warns that the crew is about to explode and presses the admiral for a decision.
independent_English: The crew's about to blow, Admiral! What are we gonna do?

source_meaning: The older speaker observes that the crew's discontent is about to erupt and asks the admiral what to do.
independent_English: The crew's fit to burst, Admiral. What do you think we ought to do?

source_meaning: A panicked younger voice says the sailors are furious and demanding that they go to port, then asks what to do.
independent_English: Admiral! The crew's really mad! They're saying we have to go to port! What do we do?

source_meaning: A polite speaker says the crew has run out of patience and asks the admiral what to do.
independent_English: Admiral, the crew's at the end of its patience. How shall we handle this?

source_meaning: The speaker orders silence and challenges anyone who defies the admiral to face them personally.
independent_English: Quiet! If you defy the admiral, you'll answer to me!

source_meaning: After a pause, the speaker tells the crew to settle down and challenges anyone who defies the admiral.
independent_English: ...Settle down! Defy the admiral and you'll have me to deal with!

source_meaning: The speaker orders obedience to the admiral and uses the first-person form IC to say they will face anyone who defies the admiral.
independent_English: Listen to the admiral! If you won't, you'll have to go through me!

source_meaning: The speaker firmly tells the crew to be quiet and says they will personally take on anyone who defies the admiral.
independent_English: That's enough! If you defy the admiral, you'll have to deal with me!

source_meaning: An impatient speaker bluntly orders the crew to shut up and personally challenges anyone who defies the admiral.
independent_English: Oh, shut up! You wanna defy the admiral? You deal with me!

source_meaning: An older voice demands obedience to the admiral and offers to deal with anyone who disobeys.
independent_English: Do as the admiral says! Anyone who won't can answer to me!

source_meaning: A youthful speaker tells the crew to behave and offers to take on anyone who refuses.
independent_English: Settle down! If you won't, you'll have to deal with me!

source_meaning: A frightened cry follows the Boarding Leader's challenge.
independent_English: Eek!

source_meaning: The immediate danger has passed for today, but the speaker advises putting into port as soon as possible.
independent_English: We're out of trouble for now, but we'd better put into port as soon as we can.

source_meaning: The speaker urges the admiral to find a port soon and says the next incident could end differently.
independent_English: ...Admiral, let's find a port soon. We don't know what'll happen next time.

source_meaning: The speaker insists they need to dock somewhere and feels sorry for the sailors.
independent_English: ...Admiral, we've got to find a port. I feel kind of sorry for the crew.

source_meaning: The speaker urges a stop in port and feels sorry for the sailors after seeing them like this.
independent_English: ...Admiral, let's put into port somewhere. I hate seeing the crew like this.

source_meaning: The speaker is relieved the immediate trouble is over, urges a quick port call, and hates having to treat their shipmates this way.
independent_English: We got through it this time... Let's find a port, quick. I hate doing this to our own crew.

source_meaning: The older speaker observes that the trouble seems to have settled, then urges a port call soon.
independent_English: Things seem to have settled down. Still, we'd best find a port soon.

source_meaning: A younger speaker is relieved, notices that everyone is on edge, and urges the admiral to dock soon.
independent_English: Oh, good... But everyone's still upset. Admiral, we'd better get to port soon.

source_meaning: The crew has calmed down this time, but the next incident is uncertain. The speaker advises putting into port promptly.
independent_English: They've settled down this time. Who knows about next time? We'd do well to find a port soon.

source_meaning: A formal warning that the crew cannot be restrained without a Boarding Leader.
independent_English: Admiral! We can't restrain the crew without a Boarding Leader!

source_meaning: A restrained speaker explains that a Boarding Leader is necessary to quell the mutiny.
independent_English: Admiral, without a Boarding Leader, we can't put down the mutiny.

source_meaning: An informal speaker insists that putting down the mutiny is impossible without a Boarding Leader.
independent_English: Admiral, there's no way we can put down a mutiny without a Boarding Leader!

source_meaning: The speaker calls it reckless to try to quell the mutiny without a Boarding Leader.
independent_English: Admiral! Trying to put down the mutiny without a Boarding Leader would be reckless!

source_meaning: A rough voice warns the admiral they cannot force the crew into submission without a Boarding Leader.
independent_English: Admiral! Without a Boarding Leader, we can't force the crew to back down!

source_meaning: The older speaker says that without a Boarding Leader, they cannot restrain the crew by force.
independent_English: Admiral, we can't subdue the crew by force without a Boarding Leader.

source_meaning: A youthful voice warns that without a Boarding Leader they cannot get the crew to obey.
independent_English: Admiral! Without a Boarding Leader, there's no way we can get the crew to listen!

source_meaning: The admiral apologizes to the sailors and offers a special meal with the usual formalities set aside for the day.
independent_English: I'm sorry, everyone. Let's forget the formalities today and share a special meal. It's my way of making it up to you.

source_meaning: After a pause, the admiral asks for more patience and offers a special meal for everyone with formalities relaxed for the day.
independent_English: ...Bear with me a little longer. For today, let's set the formalities aside. I'll treat you all to a special meal!

source_meaning: The admiral gently asks the sailors to be patient and tries to lift their spirits by suggesting an enjoyable meal together.
independent_English: Hang in there a little longer, okay? Let's all sit down to a good meal today. That ought to lift your spirits!

source_meaning: The admiral asks the crew to bear with her a little longer and offers everyone a special meal by way of making up for it.
independent_English: Please bear with me a little longer. To make it up to you, I'll treat everyone to a special meal today.

source_meaning: A sailor angrily rejects the offer and refuses to be taken in by it.
independent_English: You think you can fool us with that?

source_meaning: A sailor tells the others to drag the admiral out and beat them up together.
independent_English: Drag the admiral out! Let's give them a beating!

source_meaning: The admiral cries out in surprise, tells the sailors to stop and exclaims at the pain.
independent_English: Whoa, stop it! Ow!

source_meaning: The admiral demands to know what the attackers are doing and cries out in pain.
independent_English: What are you doing? Ow!

source_meaning: The admiral gives a startled cry, tells them to stop and exclaims at the pain.
independent_English: Aah! Stop it! Ow!

source_meaning: After a pause and a cry of pain, the admiral firmly orders the attackers to stop.
independent_English: ...Ow! Stop that!

source_meaning: The speaker demands an end to it and asks whether the sailors have had enough.
independent_English: That's enough! Had enough yet?

source_meaning: The speaker firmly orders the sailors to stop.
independent_English: That's enough! Stop it!

source_meaning: The speaker tells the sailors to stop and asks whether hitting the admiral was enough to satisfy them.
independent_English: Stop it! You've already hit the admiral. Haven't you had enough?

source_meaning: The speaker tells the sailors to stop and says they went too far by laying hands on the admiral.
independent_English: Enough, all of you! You went too far when you laid hands on the admiral!

source_meaning: An older voice demands they stop and asks whether laying hands on the admiral was still not enough.
independent_English: That's enough! You laid hands on the admiral. Still not satisfied?

source_meaning: A youthful voice repeatedly protests and asks the attackers to show the admiral some sympathy.
independent_English: Stop it, I said! Can't you see what you're doing to the admiral?

source_meaning: A forceful speaker demands an end and asks whether the sailors have had enough.
independent_English: Enough! That should've satisfied you by now!

source_meaning: The assigned cook agrees and takes responsibility for preparing the meal.
independent_English: Understood. Leave the cooking to me!

source_meaning: The speaker accepts and uses the first-person form IC to take responsibility for the rest.
independent_English: Got it! Leave the rest to me!

source_meaning: The speaker accepts and asks to be left in charge of the rest.
independent_English: Understood! I'll take it from here.

source_meaning: A rough voice accepts and says the rest can be left to him.
independent_English: Right! Leave the rest to me!

source_meaning: The older speaker agrees and asks to be trusted with the rest.
independent_English: Very well. Leave it to me.

source_meaning: The younger speaker gladly accepts and says food is something they can take care of.
independent_English: Sure! If it's food you need, leave it to me!

source_meaning: A polite speaker acknowledges the order and takes responsibility for the rest.
independent_English: Understood. I'll see to the rest!

source_meaning: A sailor approves of the admiral's response and says the admiral knows how to listen to reason.
independent_English: Now that's our admiral! You know how to listen to reason!
